title: Bhai Lalo's bread
hookLine: at Saidpur he eats the coarse bread of Lalo the carpenter and turns down the rich Malik Bhago's feast

cards: Two invitations, the same night. One is from the richest man in town: a long table, silver dishes, the important people of the district, and being seen there would do your reputation a lot of good.

The other is from a carpenter in a small house at the edge of town. He's offering what he has: a few pieces of coarse, heavy bread. Guru Nanak got both invitations, tradition says, in a town called Saidpur, in the Punjab.
The rich man was an official named Malik Bhago. The carpenter was named Lalo. And the whole town was watching to see which door the holy man would walk through.

teach.h: HE WENT TO THE CARPENTER'S HOUSE.
teach.b: Nanak went to Lalo's. He stayed with the carpenter, sat on his floor and ate his bread, rough, tradition says, made from coarse grain. Malik Bhago was offended.
He'd laid on a feast, and his visitor had gone to a laborer's hut instead. So he sent for Nanak and demanded to know why.
The answer, as Sikhs tell it, was simple: Lalo's bread is earned by honest work, with his own hands.

teach.h: THE FEAST WAS PAID FOR BY THE POOR.
teach.b: Your feast, the Guru said, was paid for by squeezing the poor. What tradition says happened next is tomorrow's story. Today, stay with the choice.
By day fourteen you'd met all three pillars: remember God's name, share what you have, and earn an honest living, kirat karni. Lalo is kirat with sawdust on his hands. He isn't a priest.
He isn't rich. He works, he earns, and he shares what he earns with a stranger at his door, and the Guru treats that coarse bread as the finest food in town. Lalo isn't only in the story.

teach.h: LALO'S NAME IS IN THE SCRIPTURE.
teach.b: He's in the scripture too: in a hymn in raga Tilang, Guru Nanak speaks to him by name, O Lalo, as if talking to a friend. A carpenter from a small town has his name in the Sikh holy book.
The bread isn't sweet because of what's in it. It's sweet because of how it was earned.

how: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, as one of the three pillars of daily life alongside remembering God's name and sharing; the story of Bhai Lalo is a sakhi often told to children.

o: skill in a craft, like a carpenter's woodwork
honest work, earning your living with your own hands
a plain meal shared with a holy guest who visits

games.q: who's who at Saidpur — tap the pairs.
p: a rich official with a feast
a hymn where Nanak says, O Lalo

s: Nanak went to the rich man's feast first
he stayed with Lalo, the carpenter, and ate his coarse bread.
Bhai Lalo is named in the Sikh scripture
Guru Nanak addresses him by name in a hymn in raga Tilang.
earning an honest living is one of three Sikh commitments
remember God's name, share, and earn honestly: kirat.

games.q: you're a visiting holy man in Saidpur. the richest man in town invites you to a feast. a carpenter offers coarse bread. where do you eat?
o: the feast: it's rude to refuse the powerful.
games.why: Nanak stayed with Lalo. when Malik Bhago demanded why, the answer was that honest bread was worth more than a feast squeezed from the poor.

practice: Bring to mind one plain meal, or hold it if it's in front of you: a slice of toast, a bowl of rice. Think of the hands it passed through, the farmer, the driver, the person at the register, maybe your own.
If you pray, give thanks in your own way; if you don't, let the plainness be enough.

wordCard.voice: Kirat. Honest work, earned with your own hands, like the coarse bread Bhai Lalo shared with Guru Nanak instead of a rich man's feast.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, honest work; kirat karni, to earn an honest living, is one of the three Sikh pillars.

carryVoice: Your line: honest bread is sweet. Tomorrow, what the Guru's hands showed Malik Bhago. Until then.
